TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
SUPREME COURT OF NEW SOUTH WALES
COURT ROOM 12D
TUESDAY, 24 FEBRUARY 2026
AT 10:30AM (AEDT)
OPENING HEARING
APPEARANCES
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC | COMMISSIONER
UNCLE ALLAN MURRAY | WELCOME TO COUNTRY
RICHARD LANCASTER SC | COUNSEL ASSISTING
Any person who publishes any part of this transcript in any way and to any person contrary
to a direction against publication commits an offence against section Royal Commissions
Act 1902 (Cth).

<THE OPENING HEARING COMMENCED AT 10:30AM
COMMISSIONER: We will commence today's proceeding by calling on Uncle
Allan Murray to give us a Welcome to Country. Uncle Allan is a Wiradjuri and a
Kamilaroi man. His father comes from the Cummeragunja village on the Murray and
was a member - or is a member of the Stolen Generation. His mother is a Kamilaroi
woman from north-western New South Wales. Uncle Allan is currently the
chairperson of the Metropolitan Local Aboriginal Land Council. So I now call on
Uncle Allan to give us a Welcome to Country.
UNCLE ALLAN MURRAY: Many thanks. In the corresponding Welcome to
Country, I want to acknowledge that we're on Gadigal land, and given the
circumstances of what occurred in December, it means that sorrow and business is
part of the way of life, as we see in Australia. But also, I want to acknowledge our
greatest warriors, Pemulwuy, Barangaroo, Musquito and Windradyne. These are our
legendary warriors who fought for this country. And a Welcome to Country is about
talking about their relationships to the land, in particular when the tall ships came
through Sydney Harbour in 1770.
We're still fighting for our land rights. We're still fighting for our sovereignty
because we never signed a piece of paper to say we had given up this land. But a
Welcome to Country is about sharing our beliefs and understanding, our customs and
our way of life, because truly we have faced many adversities over the past since
1770, and we know that atrocities have been committed against us and we're still
wanting a reckoning.
Like yourselves, you're finding the reckoning and a solution to the problems we've
faced every day since 1770 about Australians respecting us and Australians
respecting all of us. And because we had a failed referendum, like yourselves, we
feel your pain, we feel your sorrow and we feel that. But a Welcome to Country is
about understanding why you come to these lands because this is the land of
opportunity, but also, it means that First Nations people from here, from Bondi to
Sydney - there are something in the order of like 54 clans that make up all the
Aboriginal clans in New South Wales - but here in Sydney we've got 29 clans and
the only two surviving clans that live today are the Gadigal People and the Bidjigal
people of La Perouse.
Myself, like the Commissioner said in the brief, she said, "My parents come from far
wider places," but because of the past policies, it means that Aboriginal people have
been flown into Sydney since 1770, pushing Aboriginal people off land, and we do
understand that. But the goodwill of us, in terms of our sorrow and our business, we
still have a reckoning. But a Welcome to Country is about exploring all this and I
wish the Commissioner well, and I hope that one day you would feel fit and proper
to conduct the proceedings on land so we can mix the dirt, smoke the bush and have
a proper smoking ceremony. So with that, good morning to you.

COMMISSIONER: Thank you for that warm, inclusive and empathetic Welcome
to Country, Uncle Allan.
This is the initial sitting of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social
Cohesion. The Commission was established by Letters Patent signed by the
Governor-General on 9 January 2026. Since that date, Letters Patent in identical
terms have been issues by the Governors of each of the States. Under each of the
Letters Patent, the Commission is required to examine and report on the matters that
are identified in four terms of reference. I don't propose to refer to all of them in full.
They can be accessed on the Commission's website. What I propose to do is to
outline the three principal terms and I'm going to do that in reverse order.
The third term requires the Commission to examine the antisemitic attack at Bondi
Beach on the 14th of December 2025, including the lead-up and planning of this
atrocity. One might expect that a Royal Commission set up to inquire into an attack
would lead evidence of it and of the heroism of those who sought to confront the
shooters, and of those who ran towards the gunfire to offer medical assistance to the
wounded. An individual has been charged with a terrorism offence with 15 counts of
murder and with 40 counts of attempted murder arising out of the attack. The trial of
that individual will be the occasion to lead evidence of the attack.
This Commission must do its work without risking any prejudice to that criminal
proceeding. Leading evidence at this Commission from people who may be
witnesses in the criminal proceeding would create that risk, and for that reason it will
not occur. I have extended an invitation, through the New South Wales Police and a
representative of the Jewish Board of Deputies to the families of the deceased and to
others directly affected by the attack to meet me later this week in less formal
surroundings so that I can explain more fully the limitations on the scope of the
matters that the Commission can address in public, having regard to the criminal
proceeding, and to enable them to ask any questions they may have about how the
Commission proposes to proceed.
The third term of reference also requires the Commission to examine the interaction
and information sharing between Commonwealth, State and Territory agencies and
between those agencies and the organisers of the Hanukkah event. The Commission
is to investigate the security arrangements for that event and to report on whether our
intelligence and law enforcement agencies performed to maximum effectiveness.
This assessment necessarily requires consideration of whether these agencies had
appropriate powers and systems, and whether the existing legislative framework and
protocols governing the release of information prevented any agency from taking
appropriate preventative action.
In this connection, the Commission is asked to identify any gaps in the legal and
regulatory frameworks that might impede the ability of law enforcement, border
control, immigration and security agencies to prevent and respond to an attack of this
character. The Commission is to deliver an interim report to the Governor-General
and the Governors of the States not later than 30 April 2026 that focuses on this third

term of reference and that identifies any issues that require urgent or immediate
action.
Mr Dennis Richardson AC had commenced inquiring into several of the matters that
are the subject of this third term of reference at the time the Commission was
established. Following its establishment, Mr Richardson agreed to continue his work
as a special adviser to the Commission. Mr Richardson is uniquely well placed to
advise on the material that the Commission should seek from our intelligence and
security agencies in order to test the effectiveness of our preparedness for a terrorist
attack. Not only as he's a former director-general of ASIO but he has a deep
understanding of the workings of the Commonwealth Government, having served as
secretary to the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Department of Defence.
Less than three weeks after the attack, Mr Richardson had notified the various
intelligence, national security and law enforcement agencies of the material that he
would need to review, in order that he could complete his inquiry. The first task
following the establishment of this Commission was to issue notices to produce,
largely in the terms that Mr Richardson had foreshadowed in his correspondence to
the agencies, to compel them to produce these materials.
Perhaps inevitably, the absorption of an administrative inquiry into this Royal
Commission has led to some delay. This is the first Royal Commission in nearly 50
years to investigate aspects of the work of the Australian intelligence community.
Intelligence agencies that might have made material available to an internal review
without the need for getting legal advice found it necessary to consider questions of
public interest immunity, statutory nondisclosure provisions and legal professional
privilege when faced with a requirement to produce the same material to an
independent Royal Commission.
The delays in obtaining and assessing material have made it unlikely that Counsel
Assisting the Commission will be in a position to adduce evidence concerning the
adequacy of the security arrangements for the Hanukkah event, and aspects of the
effectiveness of the work of intelligence and law enforcement agencies, before the
deadline for the production of the interim report. That evidence may end up being led
after the interim report is delivered, and in that case, it will form part of the final
report. An evident purpose of requiring the preparation of an interim report is to
identify matters that require urgent or immediate action, whether that's legislative or
administrative. I am confident of being in a position to do that by 30 April 2026.
The Commission's second term of reference requires it to make recommendations to
assist law enforcement, border control, immigration and security agencies to tackle
antisemitism. In addressing this term, the Commission will look at the training of
officers of those agencies on how they should respond to antisemitic conduct or the
risk of that conduct. Importantly, the Commission will review protective security for
Jewish places of worship, major sites, educational and cultural facilities, public
events and community leaders.

The first term of reference is a broad one. It requires the Commission to investigate
the nature and prevalence of antisemitism in institutions and society by examining its
key drivers in Australia, including religious and ideologically motivated extremism
and radicalisation. The Commission is to report on the ways in which governments
can respond to antisemitism. Allied to this is the fourth term of reference which
permits me to make other recommendations arising out of the inquiry that would
contribute to strengthening social cohesion and countering the spread of
ideologically and religiously motivated extremism.
The starting point in addressing this first term of reference requires an understanding
of what constitutes antisemitism. This is not a subject that is free of controversy. The
International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, which from now on I shall refer to
as IHRA, has developed a non-legally binding working definition of antisemitism.
This is a definition that has been adopted by many liberal democracies. It was
adopted by the Australian Government in October 2021 under Prime Minister
Morrison, and following the May 2022 federal election Prime Minister Albanese
affirmed that adoption. The IHRA definition has been adopted or is supported by the
governments of the States.
It's the function of this Commission to make recommendations to governments about
how best to tackle antisemitism, and it makes evident sense for the Commission to
apply the same definition as the Commonwealth and the States in formulating these
recommendations. It follows that in investigating the nature and prevalence of
antisemitism in Australia, the Commission will apply the IHRA working definition.
The definition itself is uncontroversial. It provides:
"Antisemitism is a certain perception of Jews which may be expressed as a hatred
towards Jews. Rhetorical and physical manifestations of antisemitism are directed
toward Jewish or non-Jewish individuals and/or their property, toward Jewish
community institutions and religious facilities."
The definition is accompanied by 11 examples of conduct which could amount to
antisemitism. At least two of the examples are controversial and have led some
critics to argue that the IHRA working definition wrongly labels as antisemitic the
expression of political views which do not reflect a hatred of Jews.
While I'm open to receiving submissions on the issue, my current view is that these
concerns pay insufficient regard to the terms of the definition itself and they're apt to
overlook the requirement to take account of the overall context in which conduct
occurs before making any determination that the conduct is antisemitic. I should note
that it is uncontroversial that criticism of the policies that may be pursued by the
government of Israel from time to time is not, of itself, antisemitic.
Examining the ways in which we might strengthen social cohesion in Australia could
well be the work of years, not months. I am required to deliver my final report to the
Governor-General and the governors of the States not later than the first anniversary

of the Bondi massacre. Anniversaries are important. The first anniversary for those
directly affected by it and for the broader Jewish and Bondi communities is going to
be a difficult time. I acknowledge that for some it will never be right to speak of
closure. But one small part of coming to terms with the events of that evening will be
the work of this Commission. I regard the delivery of my report on or before the first
anniversary as a matter of critical importance.
This imposes a tight time frame and it's going to impose limitations on how the
Commission approaches its terms of reference. My focus will be a practical one. I
encourage members of the community who have an interest in any of the
Commission's terms of reference to visit the Commission's website. A submission
can be made by any person using the online form or by email. I am interested in
hearing from Jewish Australians who have experienced antisemitism, whether at
school or at university or in the workplace or elsewhere.
Making a submission does not commit a person to giving evidence in public and no
person will be pressured to do so, but I am confident that there will be members of
the Jewish community who are willing to give evidence in public about their
experiences of antisemitism and that their accounts may be illustrative of wider
patterns. In this way, the Commission will seek to assess the impact of antisemitism
on the daily life of Jewish Australians, and this is an important aspect of the first
term of reference.
I am mindful that while antisemitism may be the oldest religious and ethnic
prejudice, other religions and ethnicities are also subject to prejudice in Australia. I
expect that social cohesion will be advanced by measures that address discrimination
against religious faiths, ethnicities and cultures generally. Nonetheless, against the
background of the massacre of innocent people who appear to have been targeted
simply because they were Jewish, I trust everyone will appreciate why the focus of
this Commission will be on tackling antisemitism as a starting point in strengthening
our bonds of social cohesion.
I will now call on Senior Counsel Assisting to outline the practices and procedures
that he proposes the Commission adopt and to give a broad indication of the nature
of the evidence that he anticipates leading before the Commission. Mr Lancaster.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you, Commissioner. I am pleased to announce
formally my appearance as Senior Counsel Assisting the Royal Commission.
Appearing with me as Senior Counsel Assisting is Ms Zelie Heger SC, and with us
Ms Tamara Phillips, Ms Eleanor Jones and Mr Joe Petry seated at the bar table
today.
The central task of the Counsel Assisting team is to assist you, Commissioner, to
inquire into the issues set out on the terms of reference and report upon them by the
dates set out in the Letters Patent. Counsel will work closely with the Solicitors
Assisting the Commission. There will be a team of solicitors ably led by Ms Louise
Amundsen and Mr Tony Giugni.

The Commission has the ongoing benefit of the vast experience of Mr Dennis
Richardson AC and those who are assisting him at the time of the commencement of
this Commission. The staff of the Commission includes analysts, researchers,
support officers and other corporate staff. The administration of the Royal
Commission is undertaken by the Office of the Official Secretary, Ms Anne Sheehan.
The antisemitic attack on Jewish Australians in Bondi on 14 December 2025 was a
truly horrifying event. Like in so many other parts of Sydney and Australia, members
of our community were enjoying a summer Sunday evening gathering at a public
park near the beach. But a Jewish celebration for Hanukkah, the Festival of Light, 15
people were killed. Many others were seriously wounded, and their lives will never
be the same. There are many people have been left with serious psychological scars
from that day.
The Counsel Assisting team acknowledge with great sadness the immense trauma
this has caused Jewish Australians, and members of the community living in Bondi,
those visiting for a meal or a swim that evening, those who bravely rushed to help
and many others throughout Sydney and Australia who have been deeply affected by
the attack.
Commissioner, you have summarised the terms of reference and they are available to
be read on the Royal Commission website, asc.royalcommission.gov.au. As you've
mentioned all six State jurisdictions have also issued terms of reference in similar
form. One benefit of that occurring is that it demonstrates a truly national imperative
to tackle antisemitism. Another is the practical benefit that you have and may
exercise the powers of a Royal Commissioner under both Commonwealth legislation
and State legislation.
The Royal Commission website is the official hub for public information about the
activities of the inquiry. In your remarks today you invited public submissions and if
any individuals or organisations wish to make a submission, please visit the website
for details about how to do so. People can also subscribe to the Royal Commission
email mailing list through the website to remain up to date with its activities.
The terms of reference stipulate that the interim report is to focus on issues requiring
urgent or immediate action. If members of the public who wish to make a submission
intend to draw attention to matters that they consider require urgent or immediate
action, the Commission should receive those submissions by the13th of March.
Otherwise, the Commission will continue to receive submissions in April and in
May.
I will now address some important aspects of the procedures of the Royal
Commission for the information of the public and for the particular attention of those
who may become more closely involved in the work of the Commission as witnesses
or interested persons or organisations. The Royal Commission has recently prepared
a number of practice notes to guide its procedures. You, Commissioner, will review

these as necessary to ensure they are promoting the efficiency and effectiveness of
Commission procedures.
These practice guidelines are, by way of brief summary, firstly, a general practice
guideline explaining the Commission and how it operates, how to communicate with
the Royal Commission and make submissions, and expectations as to how evidence
before the Commission will be published. This also explains how confidentiality
applications might be made.
The second is a guideline covering hearings which explains the way in which
hearings are expected to run, the process of obtaining leave to appear before the
Commission and the process for examining and cross-examining any witnesses
called.
The third practice note is a document production guideline which explains the
mechanics for producing material to the Commission, including how to make claims
of confidentiality over documentary material that is produced. This guideline
contains a detailed document production protocol which explains how documents
should be saved and coded for upload via the Commission's electronic systems. The
work of the Commission will certainly proceed more efficiently if the procedures in
this guideline are followed. Finally, there is a guideline addressing how claims for
legal professional privilege will be dealt with by the Commission.
Can I add that in relation to leave to appear before the Royal Commission, in due
course the Solicitors Assisting the Commission will fix a time for the submission of
applications for leave to appear. This will be notified. In the usual course such
applications will be dealt with by the Commissioner on the papers in advance of a
relevant hearing.
As you have indicated, Commissioner, the terms of reference require questions to be
asked and answered about antisemitism in Australia leading up to the attack and
about the steps taken by law enforcement and security agencies to protect the
community. There is one important issue that must be addressed immediately and
publicly. You have done so, but I do wish to repeat it. It's also an issue that is
relevant to the scope and content of the interim report due on 30 April.
The Letters Patent refer to:
"The necessity for the inquiry to be conducted in a manner that does not occasion
prejudice to current or future criminal proceedings or national security or undermine
social cohesion."
As you've mentioned and as is widely known, the Commonwealth Director of Public
Prosecutions is currently prosecuting criminal proceedings against an accused person
who is charged with committing a terrorist act, 15 counts of murder, 40 counts of
attempted murder and other offences. The currency of the prosecution and the nature
of the charges brought against the accused are such that it is not possible for this

Commission to inquire into and report on a number of the elements of term of
reference (c) which, as you have summarised, is the third term of reference
concerning the circumstances of the Bondi attack.
This Commission and the steps it takes in its important work of gathering evidence
will not interfere with the administration of justice or otherwise prejudice that
prosecution. Receipt of evidence from those who may be witnesses in the criminal
proceedings would carry that risk and, as you've indicated, Commissioner, that will
not be done. For the same reason, we do not propose to conduct public hearings on
the matters with which those pending charges are concerned, and judgment will need
to be exercised about where that line is to be drawn. This will inevitably reduce the
scope of the Commission's public hearings and the Commissioner's public reports on
some issues, but it is necessary to preserve the proper administration of criminal
justice.
Turning now to evidence gathering to support the report and recommendations of the
Royal Commission, the Counsel Assisting team will lead evidence relevant to the
terms of reference. A great deal of the evidence will be documentary. This
Commission has already issued dozens of notices to produce to Commonwealth and
State agencies and various other organisations of interest. Some documents have
been produced and continue to be produced in answer to those notices to produce.
There are also further notices to produce that are yet to be issued.
It is also proposed to lead evidence from relevant persons by way of witness
statements. The Commission will also hear oral evidence from witnesses in person,
including expert evidence. The process of document production by some recipients
of notices is not presently where we would like it to be. Commissioner, in light of the
very tight timeline within which you are required to inquire and report, it is
appropriate for you, in my submission, not to countenance any delay at all in the
production of documents or witness statements that are required to be produced. The
Royal Commissions Act 1902 of the Commonwealth and relevant State equivalent
legislation contain ample powers to require the attendance of witnesses to explain
any delay.
Counsel Assisting propose to lead evidence on at least the following four broad
topics. The first is to identify antisemitic conduct in its various forms in Australian
society, including by hearing from Jewish Australians about their own lived and
living experiences of antisemitism. This will examine the large number and
increasing prominence of antisemitic incidents in Australia in recent years and,
indeed, in recent days.
The second broad topic is to inquire into the drivers of antisemitism, including
ideologically and religiously motivated extremism, radicalisation pathways and
vectors for extremist content online and in institutions. This will include considering
the actions of individuals or groups professing racist or far-right ideology or extreme
cultural or religious prejudice. The Commission will explore ways to counter the
spread of extremism in Australia.

The fourth broad topic is to identify what law enforcement and security agencies
have been doing to tackle antisemitic conduct and how the response could be
improved for the protection of the community. And the fourth broad topic is an
inquiry into the circumstances leading up to and surrounding the attack on 14
December. Subject to what I've said earlier about being careful not to prejudice the
criminal proceeding, this will include an inquiry into threat assessments and
information sharing by agencies, the steps taken by agencies in response to the
planned event at Bondi and to secure it, and steps taken in response to the attack
itself.
The Royal Commission has already commenced informing itself about many of these
topics, including by informal meetings and roundtables with numerous individuals
and organisations. Counsel Assisting look forward to continuing that process and to
working closely with interested community organisations to advance the work of the
Commission.
The Letters Patent refer to social cohesion as the national consensus in support of
democracy, freedom and the rule of law. The consensus to which the Letters Patent
refer is not a uniformity of opinion. Nor does it require or involve the suppression of
fair criticism and debate. It is quite the opposite, in my submission. It is a consensus
that a diverse multicultural society can subsist and thrive only by mutual acceptance
of our respective democratic freedoms exercised according to law. Social cohesion
begins with empathy. A large part of the work of this Commission will be to present
evidence to allow a broader understanding of the scourge of antisemitism, its nature
and prevalence throughout Australian society, and its impact on the lives of fellow
Australians. Through that understanding there may be opportunities to improve.
The schedule of hearing days on which the Royal Commission will sit in public to
hear evidence has not yet been fixed. Hearing days will be notified on the Royal
Commission website. That process will begin as soon as practicable having regard to
the production of relevant documents and witness statements and the requirements of
procedural fairness.
The terms of reference require an inquiry into very substantial issues in a short space
of time. Commissioner, the final product of the Royal Commission will be your
report and the recommendations you make to the Commonwealth and State
governments. The consideration and implementation of those recommendations will
be a matter for those governments. In my submission, the Commission ought now be
adjourned to a date to be fixed.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you, Mr Lancaster. The Commission will now adjourn
to a date to be fixed.
<THE HEARING ADJOURNED AT 11.06 AM
